hits.name: Rowan Cheung
hits.text:
A ton of AI announcements from OpenAI, Nvidia, Microsoft, and Google in the past 48 hours.

Here's everything going on in AI right now:

1. California sued OpenAI over the July incident where its AI agents hacked Hugging Face. Between the growing number of escapes, rogue agent "swarms," and AI-assisted hacks, the public likely only knows a fraction of what’s actually happening.

2. Jensen Huang made his first public statement since resigning as Nvidia CEO, apologizing for his "serious mistakes" and saying he'd be honored to return. A source told CNBC the board is focused on whether his conduct put national security at risk. Trump said he "would not mind" (but still backs Tim Cook for the job).

3. OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. Astra now sits ahead of Google's Gemini 4 Carbon and behind only Claude Fable 5.2 on Artificial Analysis. Testers were not happy though, with one calling it "the worst model OpenAI has ever released." Probably not what OpenAI was hoping for ahead of Anthropic's IPO.

4. The U.S. is reportedly set to label more than 24 AI firms (including Nvidia, OpenAI, and Anthropic) as "national champions," with faster chip export approvals and federal financing to sell American AI abroad. The goal is a one-stop shop where foreign buyers can get U.S. chips, data centers, and models as a bundle, rather than turning to Chinese rivals like Huawei.

5. OpenAI published a study of 1,800+ scientists using ChatGPT, who say AI lets them work about 2x faster at the same quality, and nearly 3x faster when writing research code. OpenAI is also opening the free program to up to 200K researchers, with applications for 50K ChatGPT Plus grants opening Nov. 23.

6. Microsoft released 7 new MAI models at Ignite. MAI Code 2 lands within a few points of Claude Opus 5.5 on coding for a twentieth of the price, and MAI Image 2.7 is now #1 on Artificial Analysis' image editing leaderboard at about a sixth of OpenAI's price.

7. Google declared that "the era of autonomous attacks has arrived," warning that hackers now use AI agents to turn new software patches into working exploits with no human involved. As the cost of intelligence continues to go down, I only expect this to get worse.

8. OpenAI signed deals with 4 outside safety groups (Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire) to test its models from inside the company, with access to source code, training data, and staff researchers.

9. Alibaba released Qwen4-Max, a flagship model it says beats Claude Opus 5.5 on 6 of 16 benchmarks. Artificial Analysis has it well behind Opus overall, though (46 vs. 59).

10. Demis Hassabis' drug discovery startup Isomorphic Labs raised $5B, saying its AI-designed cancer and immune disease candidates are nearing human trials. Really exciting step forward towards the goal of curing all diseases with AI.

11. Google started rolling out Gemini's Tasks mode free in 6 countries, letting the assistant phone businesses, book appointments, and shop for you with its new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model.

12. Perplexity launched Frontier Research, a new team that will openly publish models and papers while working toward AI that can do research on its own.

...daily reminder that this is the worst AI will ever be.

hits.name: Tibor Blaho
hits.text:
I've been testing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on my day-to-day work

Most of what I gave them, small or bigger tasks, they got done - finding out why something broke, managing servers across multiple data centers, building new projects, fixing defects, reviewing changes, taking care of backups and monitoring

Also smaller tasks like research, admin and office work

During testing of GPT-6 Astra, it moved a nearly 20-year-old codebase from one version control system to another including the complete history 

This time I asked the new Astra to upgrade that same multimillion-line legacy app, with its legacy dependencies, from a very outdated version of its programming language to the current one

After about 3 hours I could already use it locally, and after about 6 hours all tests passed from a clean checkout

There's of course still more work to do, but the first results are very promising

I used them mostly in the Codex app and in T3 Code, which I now prefer for most of my work

T3 Code runs on my Mac, and I can connect to it from my Omarchy machine or from the iOS app over VPN and continue where I left off

I use Codex and Claude Code directly from T3 Code, so I can hand off between them and orchestrate subagents across both, because I use Astra together with Fable & Opus

I let one do the research and give its findings to the other to see what it missed, to brainstorm how to fix something or how to approach a problem

They also review each other's work - Astra still finds defects in Fable's code and Fable still finds defects in Astra's code

So it still makes sense to use both in my opinion, for me Astra and Fable are the best team currently available

Every new model works and communicates a bit differently than the one before, and so far adapting how I use it was enough for me to work well with it

Pro 200 gets Ultrafast for the first time (with Sol), and Pro 500 gets it with both Astra and Sol

Astra is also 20% cheaper in the API now - $8 input and $40 output per 1M tokens

For my work these are good models - I'll keep using Astra and move my other tasks to the new Sol

hits.name: Avi Chawla
hits.text:
Autoregressive LLMs vs. diffusion LLMs, clearly explained:

(a popular LLM interview question)

Generating 500 tokens doesn't always require 500 sequential decoding steps.

Autoregressive models extend a response one token at a time. Masked diffusion models can predict multiple positions together, then repeat that process to complete the response.

Both can use transformer components such as embeddings, attention, and feed-forward layers. Their attention patterns and training objectives differ.

1) Autoregressive LLMs

In standard autoregressive decoding, each forward pass produces a probability distribution for the next token.

The selected token is appended, and generation continues from that longer sequence.

Causal attention prevents a position from accessing future positions. Earlier token representations therefore stay unchanged as new tokens arrive.

That allows their KV to be cached and reused.

A 500-token response normally requires 500 sequential token-generation steps, although techniques such as speculative decoding can reduce expensive model passes.

2) Diffusion LLMs

In the masked diffusion approach shown below, generation starts with masked output positions alongside the prompt.

A denoising pass predicts candidate tokens for multiple positions using bidirectional context.

With confidence-based sampling, selected predictions are retained while other positions remain masked for subsequent steps.

The model progressively fills the sequence. It doesn't necessarily produce a complete draft and repeatedly rewrite every token.

Some implementations generate block by block rather than processing the entire response together.

Multiple tokens can be finalized per step, allowing fewer steps than output tokens. The step budget affects both speed and quality.

There are some engineering tradeoffs.

Bidirectional attention makes standard autoregressive KV reuse harder. A token's representation can change when surrounding positions are updated, even if that token itself stays fixed.

Caching therefore depends on the architecture and decoding strategy. Block diffusion, for example, can support KV caching across completed blocks.

Fewer steps also don't guarantee lower latency. Each step may process many positions, so total computation and implementation matter.

Bidirectional conditioning also supports filling gaps in text or code.

I covered how KV reuse works in autoregressive decoding in a separate breakdown.

It covers what gets cached during prefill, how the cache grows during decoding, and why it becomes the main memory bottleneck at long context.

Read it below.

The model progressively fills the sequence. It doesn't necessarily produce a complete draft and repeatedly rewrite every token.

Some implementations generate block by block rather than processing the entire response together.

Multiple tokens can be finalized per step, allowing fewer steps than output tokens. The step budget affects both speed and quality.

There are some engineering tradeoffs.

Bidirectional attention makes standard autoregressive KV reuse harder. A token's representation can change when surrounding positions are updated, even if that token itself stays fixed.

Caching therefore depends on the architecture and decoding strategy. Block diffusion, for example, can support KV caching across completed blocks.

Fewer steps also don't guarantee lower latency. Each step may process many positions, so total computation and implementation matter.

Bidirectional conditioning also supports filling gaps in text or code.

I covered how KV reuse works in autoregressive decoding in a separate breakdown.

It covers what gets cached during prefill, how the cache grows during decoding, and why it becomes the main memory bottleneck at long context.

Once you have the factory-as-code foundations in place, you need the tools to measure and improve coding agent throughput:

1. Online evals and scorers: use LLM-as-a-judge to score past agent runs along dimensions you might want to improve (e.g. “Is the agent writing redundant tests? Is it producing designs that align with our style guide?”)
2. Self-improvement loops: agents that examine past eval results looking for opportunities to improve the factory code definition.
3. Benchmarks: rerun sets of agent tasks from their original state with different factory configurations (e.g. different models or skill definitions) to determine which is optimal.
4. Model routing: apply the results of evals and benchmarks to a model routing strategy that is optimized for your team’s own workflows.
5. A/B tests: prove that the factory code is optimal on a go-forward basis by running controlled split tests.

Whereas in the past we all learned to use linters, profilers, and debuggers, factory engineers should be learning these new tools today.

It's always difficult to shut down gracefully but Mem seems to be doing a better job than most. Their site offers export options and migration guides for Obsidian and other apps.

Looking back at the history of the company, I was surprised to find they'd raised $29 million in funding. That made Mem among the most funded VCware apps in the space. For comparison:

- Notion: $340m (that we know of)
- Evernote: $290m
- Mem: $29m
- Tana: $25m
- Craft: $20.8m
- Anytype: $13.4m
- Roam: $9m
- Logseq: $4.1m
- Obsidian: $0

I have always admired @_ericaxu and @shida_li for knowing early that they would shun the VC path and build Obsidian without investors.

Having watched the downfall of Evernote from afar, and experienced the pressures of VC first hand, I was afraid they might be swayed by investors waving big checks at their noses. It's one of the reasons I wanted to join Obsidian because I felt it was possible to build a 100% user-supported company in this space.

Being bootstrapped has many downsides. It means Obsidian can't subsidize pricing, can't make big speculative bets, can't hire as many people, can't parallelize projects as much...

There is certainly survivorship bias, but as I look at the landscape six years after launch, Obsidian is still alive and well. I think building without investors made us stronger.

It's a twist of irony that OpenAI's VC fund was one of the biggest investors in Mem, yet the app never adopted Markdown as a storage format.

I could have never predicted that Markdown would become as popular as it is today. Even before LLMs, I felt confident .md files would outlive Obsidian. Now I feel more confident than ever that "File over app" is a philosophy that will outlive us all.
